claim: CA1 pyramidal neurons express functional kainate receptors
source: CA1 pyramidal neurons express functional kainate receptors (Bureau et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bureau et al., 1999

claim: No detectable synaptic KAR-mediated responses can be detected in CA1 pyramidal neurons
source: However, no detectable synaptic KAR-mediated responses can be detected (Bureau et al., 1999; Castillo et al., 1997; Granger et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bureau et al., 1999; Castillo et al., 1997; Granger et al., 2013

claim: Neto1 overexpression had no effect on the size of the synaptic response recorded at −70 mV
source: Neither Neto1 (Figure 1A1) nor Neto2 (Figure 1B1) had any effect on the size of the synaptic response recorded at −70 mV
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A1 and 1B1

claim: Neto1 overexpression had no effect on the NMDA receptor response recorded at +40 mV
source: Neither Neto1 (Figure 1A1) nor Neto2 (Figure 1B1) had any effect on the size of the synaptic response recorded at −70 mV or the NMDA receptor (NMDAR) response recorded at +40 mV (Figure 1A2 and B2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A2 and B2

claim: Neto1 overexpression had no effect on paired-pulse ratio
source: Moreover, overexpression had no effect on paired-pulse ratio, a measure of presynaptic release probability (Neto1 vs control: 1.29 ± 0.11 vs 1.23 ± 0.08, p>0.05; Neto2 vs control: 1.56 ± 0.08 vs 1.46 ± 0.1, p>0.05).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of paired-pulse ratio

claim: GYKI53655 completely blocked the responses in Neto1 expressing neurons
source: The antagonist completely blocked the responses both in Neto1 (Figure 1A1) and Neto2 (Figure 1B1) expressing neurons
evidence: Supported by experimental data with GYKI53655 application shown in Figure 1A1 and 1B1

claim: Neto proteins cannot promote incorporation of the endogenous KARs into synapses
source: The antagonist completely blocked the responses both in Neto1 (Figure 1A1) and Neto2 (Figure 1B1) expressing neurons, suggesting that Neto proteins cannot promote incorporation of the endogenous KARs into synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the complete blockade of responses by GYKI53655 in Neto-expressing neurons

claim: GluK1 expression alone did not affect the size of the response recorded at −70 mV
source: We thus expressed GluK1, but this did not affect the size of the response recorded at −70 mV (Figure 1C1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C1

claim: GluK1 expression alone did not affect the NMDAR response
source: We thus expressed GluK1, but this did not affect the size of the response recorded at −70 mV (Figure 1C1) or the NMDAR response (Figure 1C2)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C2

claim: GluK1 expression alone did not affect paired-pulse ratio
source: We thus expressed GluK1, but this did not affect the size of the response recorded at −70 mV (Figure 1C1) or the NMDAR response (Figure 1C2), as well as the paired-pulse ratio (GluK1 vs control: 1.89 ± 0.17 vs 1.89 ± 0.22, p>0.05).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of paired-pulse ratio

claim: GYKI53655 fully blocked the EPSCs in GluK1-expressing neurons, indicating that functional KARs were not recruited to the synapse
source: Furthermore, GYKI53655 fully blocked the EPSCs indicating that functional KARs were not recruited to the synapse.
evidence: Supported by experimental data with GYKI53655 application

claim: Expression of GluK1 together with Neto1 resulted in a large increase in the size of synaptic response recorded at −70 mV
source: We next expressed GluK1 together with Neto1 and in this case there was a large increase in the size of synaptic response recorded at −70 mV and GYKI53655 only partially blocked the response (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: GYKI53655 only partially blocked the response in GluK1/Neto1 expressing neurons
source: We next expressed GluK1 together with Neto1 and in this case there was a large increase in the size of synaptic response recorded at −70 mV and GYKI53655 only partially blocked the response (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: 100 μM GYKI53655 blocks approximately 20% of KAR mediated responses
source: We selected a concentration of 100 μM GYKI53655 to ensure that all AMPARs were blocked (Bleakman et al., 1996). This concentration, however, will block approximately 20% of KAR mediated responses (Bleakman et al., 1996)
evidence: Supported by citation to Bleakman et al., 1996

claim: Expression of GluK1 together with Neto2 greatly increased the synaptic response
source: These experiments were repeated by expressing GluK1 along with Neto2. As reported previously (Granger et al., 2013) the synaptic response was greatly increased and GYKI53655 only partially blocked the response (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and citation to Granger et al., 2013

claim: Sparse expression of GluK1 receptors in CA1 neurons has no effect on presynaptic release probability
source: Although presynaptic KARs are known to regulate glutamate release at mossy fibers, sparse expression of GluK1 receptors in CA1 neurons has no effect on presynaptic release probability as there is no significant change of paired-pulse ratio (GluK1/Neto1 vs control: 1.46 ± 0.18 vs 1.7 ± 0.26, p>0.05; GluK1/Neto2 vs control: 1.36 ± 0.12 vs 1.52 ± 0.16, p>0.05).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of paired-pulse ratio

claim: Synaptic KAR responses are only observed when GluK1 is expressed along with either Neto1 or Neto2
source: These findings and those in Figure 1 are summarized in Figure 2C, showing that synaptic KAR responses are only observed when GluK1 is expressed along with either Neto1 or Neto2.
evidence: Supported by experimental data summarized in Figure 2C

claim: Synaptic activity is not required for Neto-dependent GluK1 synaptic trafficking
source: However, the receptor antagonists did not prevent the synaptic incorporation of either GluK1/Neto1 or GluK1/Neto2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that synaptic activity is not required for Neto-dependent GluK1 synaptic trafficking.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Expression of GluK1 with Neto1 resulted in a significant increase in the size of the NMDAR EPSCs
source: Interestingly, when GluK1 was expressed along with Neto1 or Neto2 there was a significant increase in the size of the NMDAR EPSCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C

claim: There was no difference in spine density in neurons expressing GluK1/Neto1 or GluK1/Neto2 compared to control
source: However, we found no difference in spine density in neurons expressing GluK1/Neto1 or GluK1/Neto2 compared to control.
evidence: Supported by spine density analysis data shown in Figure 3A and B

claim: There was no significant difference in the AMPAR-mediated responses between control and experimental neurons expressing GluK1 with Neto1 in the presence of ACET
source: To address these questions we expressed GluK1 with either Neto1 (Figure 3C) or Neto2 (Figure 3D) and recorded synaptic responses in the presence of the GluK1 selective antagonist ACET. In this case there was no significant difference in the AMPAR-mediated responses between control and experimental neurons
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and 3D

claim: AMPARs are not displaced by the synaptic expression of KARs
source: In this case there was no significant difference in the AMPAR-mediated responses between control and experimental neurons, indicating that AMPARs are not displaced by the synaptic expression of KARs.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of change in AMPAR-mediated responses in the presence of ACET

claim: In cells expressing GluK1 and Neto1, there was no change in quantal size
source: In cells expressing GluK1 and Neto1, we observed no change in quantal size (Figure 4A2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A1

claim: In cells expressing GluK1 and Neto1, there was a large increase in frequency of asynchronous EPSCs
source: In cells expressing GluK1 and Neto1, we observed no change in quantal size (Figure 4A2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A1), but a large increase in frequency (Figure 4A3 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A3 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A2

claim: Expression of KARs results in synapse unsilencing
source: These results tell us that expression of KARs results in synapse unsilencing.
evidence: Inferred from the increase in aEPSC frequency without change in amplitude

claim: The increase in aEPSC frequency in the GluK1/Neto1-expressing neurons was no longer observed in the presence of ACET
source: In the presence of ACET the increase in aEPSC frequency in the GluK1/Neto1-expressing neurons (Figure 4A3) was no longer observed (Figure 4B2-C2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B2-C2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B2

claim: There was no reduction in the size of aEPSCs in the presence of ACET
source: Importantly we saw no reduction in the size of aEPSCs (Figure 4C1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B1

claim: Synaptic GluK1 and AMPARs do not co-localize at the same synapses
source: The lack of change in aEPSC size in ACET (Figure 4C1, Figure 5B2, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D1), indicates that synaptic GluK1 and AMPARs do not co-localize at the same synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of change in aEPSC size in ACET

claim: KARs are excluded from synapses that are already populated with AMPARs
source: Taken together, these results suggest that KARs are excluded from synapses that are already populated with AMPARs.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of aEPSC changes with and without ACET

claim: KARs selectively populate synapses that lack AMPARs, i.e. silent synapses
source: Rather they appear to selectively populate synapses that lack AMPARs, i.e. silent synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of aEPSC changes with and without ACET

claim: The average size of GluK1-mediated quantal events is the same as the AMPAR-mediated events
source: Perhaps even more intriguing is that the average size of GluK1-mediated quantal events is the same as the AMPAR-mediated events.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on aEPSC amplitudes

claim: Deletion of the entire C-tail (Δ161) of Neto1 prevents the targeting of GluK1 receptors to the synapse
source: Deletion of the entire C-tail (Δ161) of Neto1 prevents the targeting of GluK1 receptors to the synapse (Figure 6A,B and H)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,B and H

claim: Deletion of the last 4 amino acids (Δ4) of Neto1 has no significant effect on GluK1 synaptic targeting
source: whereas deletion of the last 4 amino acids (Δ4), a putative PDZ binding motif, has no significant effect (Figure 6F and H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F and H

claim: Deletion of the last 20 amino acids (Δ20) of Neto1 has a substantial effect on synaptic GluK1 currents
source: Deletion of the last 20 amino acids (Δ20) of Neto1 has a substantial effect on synaptic GluK1 currents (Figure 6E and H)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and H

claim: The last 20 amino acids of Neto1 are critical for the synaptic incorporation of functional GluK1 receptors
source: These truncation experiments suggest that the last 20 amino acids of Neto1 are critical for the synaptic incorporation of functional GluK1 receptors.
evidence: Inferred from the truncation experiments showing effects of Δ20 deletion

claim: The Neto1S3Y/A mutant disrupted GluK1 synaptic expression to the same extent as deleting the last 20 amino acids
source: We therefore mutated three serines and a tyrosine in this region to alanines simultaneously (S3Y/A) and found that the Neto1S3Y/A mutant disrupted GluK1 synaptic expression to the same extent as deleting the last 20 amino acids (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G and H

claim: Deletion of the entire C-terminal domain (Δ148) of Neto2 fully diminished GluK1 receptor synaptic targeting
source: Deletion of the entire C-terminal domain (Δ148) fully diminished GluK1 receptor synaptic targeting by Neto2 (Figure 7A,B and I)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A,B and I

claim: Deleting the last 4 amino acids (Δ4) of Neto2 has no effect on the function of Neto2
source: whereas deleting the last 4 amino acids (Δ4) has no effect on the function of Neto2 (Figure 7F and I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F and I

claim: The last 86 amino acids of Neto2 are critical for the incorporation of synaptic GluK1 receptors
source: These results indicate that the last 86 amino acids of Neto2 are critical for the incorporation of synaptic GluK1 receptors.
evidence: Inferred from the truncation experiments showing effects of Δ86 deletion

claim: Deletion of the region between 86 and 74 amino acids (Δ86-74) of Neto2 significantly impaired Neto2-regulated GluK1 synaptic targeting
source: Of particular importance is the region between 86 and 74 amino acids (Δ86-74) as its deletion significantly impaired Neto2-regulated GluK1 synaptic targeting (Figure 7G and I)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G and I

claim: Deletion of last 74 amino acids (Δ74) of Neto2 has no significant effect on GluK1-mediated synaptic response
source: whereas deletion of last 74 amino acids (Δ74) has no significant effect on GluK1-mediated synaptic response (Figure 7E and I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E and I

claim: The Neto2S4T/A mutant impaired GluK1 synaptic expression to the same extent as the critical deletion mutant (Δ86-74)
source: Furthermore, mutation of the serines in this region as well as the threonine just next to this region to alanines (S4T/A) also impaired GluK1 synaptic expression to the same extent as this critical deletion mutant (Δ86-74) (Figure 7H and I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7H and I

claim: In wild type patches from CA1 neurons, no glutamate-evoked current was detected
source: In wild type patches from CA1 neurons, we were unable to detect any glutamate-evoked current (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A

claim: In neurons expressing only GluK1, small but significant glutamate evoked currents were observed
source: In neurons expressing only GluK1 we saw small, but significant, glutamate evoked currents
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A

claim: In patches from neurons co-expressing either Neto1 or Neto2 with GluK1, very large currents were recorded
source: whereas in patches from neurons co-expressing either Neto1 or Neto2 with GluK1 very large currents were recorded (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A

claim: Both Neto1S3Y/A and Neto2S4T/A mutants generated currents in outside-out patches of similar size to those generated by wild type Neto1 and Neto2
source: Indeed, both Neto1S3Y/A and Neto2S4T/A mutants generated currents in outside-out patches of similar size to those generated by wild type Neto1 and Neto2 (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A

claim: There is a role for Neto auxiliary proteins in targeting surface GluK1 receptors to synapses
source: These results provide strong evidence that there is, in fact, a role for these auxiliary proteins in targeting surface GluK1 receptors to synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mutants with impaired synaptic targeting maintain surface expression

claim: In the absence of Netos, the surface labeling of GluK1 was very weak
source: In the absence of Netos, the surface labeling was very weak, although the neuron clearly expressed GluK1 (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 8B

claim: In the presence of either Neto1 or Neto2, GluK1 was abundantly expressed on the surface
source: However, in the presence of either Neto1 or Neto2, GluK1 was abundantly expressed on the surface (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 8B and C

claim: Both Neto1 and Neto2 can drive the robust surface expression of GluK1
source: Together, these results indicate that both Neto1 and Neto2 can drive the robust surface expression of GluK1.
evidence: Inferred from the immunolabeling and electrophysiology data

claim: Neto1 had no effect on the deactivation of GluK1-mediated currents
source: Neto1 had no effect on the deactivation of GluK1-mediated currents, but Neto2 did slow deactivation (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D

claim: Neto2 slowed deactivation of GluK1-mediated currents
source: Neto1 had no effect on the deactivation of GluK1-mediated currents, but Neto2 did slow deactivation (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D

claim: Neto1 enhanced the rate of desensitization of GluK1-mediated currents
source: By contrast, Neto1 enhanced the rate of desensitization, whereas Neto2 slowed the rate of desensitization (Figure 8E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8E

claim: Neto2 slowed the rate of desensitization of GluK1-mediated currents
source: By contrast, Neto1 enhanced the rate of desensitization, whereas Neto2 slowed the rate of desensitization (Figure 8E), in agreement with previous results (Copits et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8E and citation to Copits et al., 2011

claim: GluK1 by itself is poorly expressed on the neuronal surface
source: We find that GluK1 by itself is poorly expressed on the neuronal surface and is not present at excitatory synapses.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on surface expression and synaptic responses

claim: GluK1 by itself is not present at excitatory synapses
source: We find that GluK1 by itself is poorly expressed on the neuronal surface and is not present at excitatory synapses.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on synaptic responses

claim: In the presence of either Neto1 or Neto2, GluK1 is expressed at very high levels on the neuronal surface
source: However, in the presence of either Neto1 or Neto2, GluK1 is expressed at very high levels on the neuronal surface and is also present at excitatory synapses.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on surface expression and synaptic responses

claim: In the presence of either Neto1 or Neto2, GluK1 is present at excitatory synapses
source: However, in the presence of either Neto1 or Neto2, GluK1 is expressed at very high levels on the neuronal surface and is also present at excitatory synapses.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on synaptic responses

claim: Neto1 and Neto2 regulate GluK1 synaptic targeting independently of their role in promoting surface trafficking
source: In addition to their role in GluK1 surface trafficking, Neto1 and Neto2 regulate its synaptic targeting independently and the underlying mechanisms for these two processes are different.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mutants with impaired synaptic targeting maintain surface expression

claim: GluK1 is excluded from synapses expressing AMPA receptors
source: Interestingly, GluK1 is excluded from synapses expressing AMPA receptors and is selectively incorporated into silent synapses.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on aEPSC patterns with and without ACET

claim: GluK1 is selectively incorporated into silent synapses
source: Interestingly, GluK1 is excluded from synapses expressing AMPA receptors and is selectively incorporated into silent synapses.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on aEPSC patterns with and without ACET

claim: Neto2, but not Neto1, slows GluK1 deactivation
source: Neto2, but not Neto1, slows GluK1 deactivation, whereas Neto1 speeds GluK1 desensitization and Neto2 slows desensitization.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on deactivation and desensitization kinetics

claim: Neto1 speeds GluK1 desensitization
source: Neto2, but not Neto1, slows GluK1 deactivation, whereas Neto1 speeds GluK1 desensitization and Neto2 slows desensitization.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on desensitization kinetics

claim: Neto2 slows GluK1 desensitization
source: Neto2, but not Neto1, slows GluK1 deactivation, whereas Neto1 speeds GluK1 desensitization and Neto2 slows desensitization.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on desensitization kinetics

claim: Neto2 has no effect on the surface expression of GluK2 in oocytes
source: Neto2 has no effect on the surface expression of GluK2 in oocytes (Zhang et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2009

claim: Neto2 has been reported to enhance surface expression of GluK1 in HEK cells and cultured neurons
source: although it has been reported to enhance surface expression of GluK1 in HEK cells and cultured neurons (Copits et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Copits et al., 2011

claim: The knock-out of Neto1 in mice does not alter the neuronal surface expression or synaptic localization of GluK2/5
source: The knock-out of Neto1 in mice does not alter the neuronal surface expression or synaptic localization of GluK2/5 (Straub et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Straub et al., 2011

claim: Other studies reported a decrease in PSD expression of GluK2 when Neto1 was knocked-out
source: although other studies reported a decrease in PSD expression of GluK2 when Neto1 was knocked-out (Tang et al., 2011; Wyeth et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tang et al., 2011; Wyeth et al., 2014

claim: Neto2 can target GluK1 to synapses of primary cultured neurons
source: Finally, it has been reported that Neto2 can target GluK1 to synapses of primary cultured neurons (Copits et al., 2011; Palacios-Filardo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Copits et al., 2011; Palacios-Filardo et al., 2014

claim: Neto1 slows deactivation and desensitization of GluK2/5
source: Neto1 slows deactivation and desensitization of GluK2/5 and deletion of Neto1 in mice speeds the decay of the KAR-mediated hippocampal mossy fiber EPSC (Straub et al., 2011; Tang et al., 2011; Wyeth et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Straub et al., 2011; Tang et al., 2011; Wyeth et al., 2014

claim: Deletion of Neto1 in mice speeds the decay of the KAR-mediated hippocampal mossy fiber EPSC
source: Neto1 slows deactivation and desensitization of GluK2/5 and deletion of Neto1 in mice speeds the decay of the KAR-mediated hippocampal mossy fiber EPSC (Straub et al., 2011; Tang et al., 2011; Wyeth et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Straub et al., 2011; Tang et al., 2011; Wyeth et al., 2014

claim: Neto2 slows deactivation and desensitization of GluK2 receptors
source: More specifically Neto2 slows deactivation and desensitization of GluK2 receptors (Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2009

claim: Neto1 speeds GluK1 desensitization, whereas Neto2 slows it
source: It has been reported that Neto1 speeds GluK1 desensitization, whereas Neto2 slows it (Copits et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Copits et al., 2011

claim: KARs are expressed postsynaptically at hippocampal CA3 mossy fiber synapses and generate a slow EPSC
source: The most studied synaptic KARs are those expressed at hippocampal CA3 mossy fiber synapses (Nicoll and Schmitz, 2005). These receptors are expressed postsynaptically and generate a slow EPSC.
evidence: Supported by citation to Nicoll and Schmitz, 2005

claim: KARs are expressed presynaptically at hippocampal CA3 mossy fiber synapses and contribute to frequency facilitation
source: They are also expressed presynaptically and contribute to the profound frequency facilitation, a hallmark of these synapses.
evidence: Supported by citation to Nicoll and Schmitz, 2005

claim: KARs are expressed postsynaptically at excitatory synapses in CA1 interneurons
source: In the CA1 region of the hippocampus, KARs are expressed postsynaptically at excitatory synapses in interneurons (Cossart et al., 1998; Frerking et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cossart et al., 1998; Frerking et al., 1998

claim: Neto1 and Neto2 are single pass transmembrane CUB domain-containing proteins
source: These neurophilin tolloid-like proteins are single pass transmembrane CUB (complement C1r/C1s, Uegf and Bmp1) domain-containing proteins.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Neto protein structure

claim: Both Neto1 and Neto2 are known to alter the kinetics of KARs
source: Both Neto1 and Neto2 are known to alter the kinetics of KARs (Copits et al., 2011; Straub et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Copits et al., 2011; Straub et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2009

claim: Organotypic hippocampal slice cultures were made from P6-P8 rats
source: Slices from P6-P8 rats were biolistically transfected with indicated plasmids together with FUGW-EGFP plasmid as a tracer on DIV 2
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: Dual whole-cell recordings were performed on DIV 8
source: Slices from P6-P8 rats were biolistically transfected with indicated plasmids together with FUGW-EGFP plasmid as a tracer on DIV 2 and then on DIV 8 dual whole-cell recordings in area CA1 were done
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: 100 μM picrotoxin was added to block inhibitory currents
source: 100 μM picrotoxin was added to block inhibitory currents and 4 μM 2-Chloroadenosine was used to control epileptiform activity.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: 4 μM 2-Chloroadenosine was used to control epileptiform activity
source: 100 μM picrotoxin was added to block inhibitory currents and 4 μM 2-Chloroadenosine was used to control epileptiform activity.
evidence: Description of experimental methods
